questions.question: What is hoisting?
questions.answer:
Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of making variable and function declarations available throughout their containing scope: before any code runs, the engine creates the bindings for those declarations, which is often described (loosely) as moving them to the top of the scope.

var declarations are hoisted and initialized with undefined; let and const are hoisted but remain in the "temporal dead zone" until their declaration line executes, so accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError.

Function declarations are hoisted along with their full definition, so they can be called before they appear in the code; function expressions and arrow functions are not. If one is assigned to a var (e.g. var foo = function() {}), only the variable foo is hoisted (as undefined), so calling foo() early throws a TypeError; with let/const it throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: Lexical scope and scope chain
questions.answer:
Lexical scope means a variable's accessibility is determined by where it is physically written in the source code, not by how the code is called. Each function creates a new scope nested inside the scope it was defined in; let/const and class declarations are additionally scoped to the nearest block ({ }), and ES modules have their own module-level scope.

When a variable is referenced, JavaScript looks it up in the current scope first, then walks outward through each enclosing (parent) scope — this ordered list of scopes is called the scope chain — until it finds the variable or reaches the global scope and throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: What are closures?
questions.answer:
A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scope even after that outer function has finished executing. In practice, the engine keeps the variables the inner function references alive for as long as that function can still be called.

Closures are commonly used for data privacy (module pattern), memoization, currying, and preserving state in event handlers or callbacks.

questions.question: Explain prototypal inheritance.
questions.answer:
In JavaScript, objects inherit properties and methods from other objects via an internal link called [[Prototype]] (accessible through Object.getPrototypeOf() or the deprecated __proto__).

When a property is accessed on an object and not found directly on it, the engine walks up the prototype chain until it finds the property or reaches null.

ES6 classes (class / extends) are syntactic sugar over this same prototype-based mechanism, not a separate classical inheritance model.

questions.question: Difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
questions.answer:
A shallow copy duplicates only the top-level properties of an object — nested objects/arrays are still shared by reference between the original and the copy, so mutating a nested value affects both. Common techniques: spread syntax ({...obj}), Object.assign(), Array.prototype.slice().

A deep copy recursively duplicates all nested structures so the copy is fully independent — achieved with structuredClone() (modern, handles most types), JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) (simple but loses functions, undefined, Date objects, etc.), or a library like Lodash's cloneDeep.

questions.question: All ES6 concepts
questions.answer:
Key ES6 (ES2015) features:

  • let/const for block scoping
  • Arrow functions with lexical this
  • Template literals
  • Default, rest, and spread parameters
  • Destructuring assignment (array and object)
  • Enhanced object literals
  • Classes (class, extends, super)
  • Promises
  • The module system (import/export)
  • Map, Set, WeakMap, WeakSet
  • Iterators and generators (function*, yield)
  • Symbol as a new primitive type
  • for...of loops (iterating over any iterable)
  • Proxy and Reflect for intercepting and customizing object operations
  • New built-in methods such as Array.from(), Object.assign(), and String.prototype.includes()

Later versions build on this — e.g. async/await (ES2017), optional chaining ?. and nullish coalescing ?? (ES2020).

questions.question: Higher-order functions
questions.answer:
A higher-order function either takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both. They enable functional composition and abstraction over behavior.

Examples: Array.prototype.map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach(), and custom utilities like a debounce(fn, delay) function that takes fn and returns a new, debounced function.

questions.question: TypeScript fundamentals and type safety
questions.answer:
TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript that compiles (transpiles) to plain JavaScript. It adds compile-time type checking — primitive types, interfaces, type aliases, generics, union/intersection types, and enums — so many bugs are caught before the code ever runs, rather than at runtime.

Type annotations, interfaces, and type aliases are erased during compilation, so they add no runtime cost (enums are the exception, since they compile to real JavaScript objects). Enabling strict mode (including strictNullChecks) is the main lever for real type safety in a codebase.

questions.question: What is the V8 JavaScript Engine?
questions.answer:
V8 is Google's open-source JavaScript (and WebAssembly) engine, written in C++, that powers Google Chrome and Node.js.

Rather than only interpreting code, V8 uses a tiered just-in-time (JIT) pipeline: the Ignition interpreter first runs JavaScript as bytecode, and frequently executed ("hot") code is then compiled to optimized native machine code by TurboFan (recent versions also add the Sparkplug and Maglev compilers as intermediate tiers). It manages memory via its own generational garbage collector.

questions.question: Difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Synchronous code executes line by line, and each statement blocks the next one until it finishes — e.g. a long-running loop freezes everything else.

Asynchronous code allows long-running operations (network requests, file I/O, timers) to be initiated and continue in the background while the main thread keeps executing other code; the result is handled later via callbacks, Promises, or async/await, without blocking the single JavaScript thread.

questions.question: Callbacks, callback hell, Promises, and async/await
questions.answer:
A callback is a function passed to another function to be invoked once an async operation completes.

"Callback hell" refers to deeply nested callbacks, each depending on the previous one's result, becoming hard to read and maintain — sometimes called the "pyramid of doom."

Promises represent a value that will be available in the future (pending/fulfilled/rejected) and allow chaining with .then()/.catch() instead of nesting.

async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises that lets asynchronous code be written and read like synchronous code, while still being non-blocking under the hood.

questions.question: Explain the JavaScript event loop step by step (Microtasks, Macrotasks, Call Stack)
questions.answer:
JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack that executes synchronous code. When an async operation (e.g. setTimeout, a Promise, or an I/O callback) completes, its callback isn't run immediately — it's placed in a queue.

The event loop continuously checks: is the call stack empty? If so, it first drains the entire microtask queue completely (Promise .then/.catch/.finally callbacks, queueMicrotask), and only then takes a single task from the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks, UI events) and pushes it onto the call stack.

This repeats indefinitely, which is why the microtask queue is fully drained (including any microtasks queued along the way) before the next task runs or the browser gets a chance to render. (The HTML spec simply calls what developers term macrotasks “tasks”.)

This describes the standard browser model. Node.js layers its own behavior on top: process.nextTick() callbacks run before Promise microtasks, and its event loop is organized into phases (timers, pending callbacks, poll, check for setImmediate, close callbacks) rather than a single macrotask queue.

questions.question: Concurrency vs. parallelism â€” why the difference matters
questions.answer:
Concurrency is about structure — dealing with multiple tasks by interleaving their progress over time, even on a single thread (which is how JavaScript's event loop achieves asynchronous behavior).

Parallelism is about execution — actually running multiple tasks at the exact same instant, which requires multiple CPU cores/threads (e.g. Node.js worker threads or the cluster module).

JavaScript's main thread is concurrent but not parallel by default; this distinction clarifies why non-blocking I/O helps throughput without multiple threads, while true CPU-bound parallel work still needs to be explicitly offloaded to workers or separate processes.

questions.question: What happens internally when a user types a URL in the browser?
questions.answer:
• Browser parses the URL and checks caches (browser, OS, router, ISP) for a DNS record.
  • If not cached, a DNS lookup resolves the domain to an IP address.
  • Browser opens a connection to that IP — a TCP connection plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, or a QUIC connection (over UDP, with TLS 1.3 built in) for HTTP/3 — reusing an existing connection when one is available.
  • Browser sends an HTTP(S) request; the server processes it and returns a response (a service worker, the HTTP cache, or a CDN edge may answer instead of the origin server).
  • Browser parses the HTML response, builds the DOM tree, and discovers/fetches linked resources (CSS, JS, images).
  • CSS is parsed into the CSSOM and combined with the DOM to build the render tree.
  • Browser performs layout (geometry) and paint (pixels), then composites layers to the screen.

questions.question: How does browser rendering work internally?
questions.answer:
The rendering engine parses HTML into a DOM tree and CSS into a CSSOM tree, combines them into a render tree (only visible nodes with computed styles), then performs layout (also called reflow) to calculate the exact position/size of each element.

This is followed by paint (filling in pixels: text, colors, images, borders) and finally composite (assembling painted layers together, often using the GPU) to produce the final frame shown on screen.

questions.question: Explain repaint vs. reflow vs. compositing.
questions.answer:
Reflow (layout) recalculates the geometry — position and size — of elements, triggered by changes like resizing or changing width/height; it's the most expensive because it can cascade to other elements.

Repaint happens when an element's appearance changes (color, background, visibility) without affecting layout — cheaper than reflow but still redraws pixels.

Compositing is the final step of combining painted layers into the final image, and browsers can composite certain properties (like transform and opacity) on the GPU without triggering layout or paint at all — which is why animating those two properties is much smoother than animating width/top.

questions.question: What causes UI jank?
questions.answer:
Jank is visible stuttering caused by the browser failing to produce a new frame within the ~16.7ms budget needed for a smooth 60fps experience.

Common causes: long-running JavaScript blocking the main thread, forced synchronous layout ("layout thrashing"), excessive DOM manipulation, large unoptimized images, animating layout-triggering properties instead of transform/opacity, and heavy garbage collection pauses.

questions.question: Explain debounce and throttle with real-world examples.
questions.answer:
Debounce delays invoking a function until a specified time has passed since the last time it was called — if the event fires again before that time elapses, the timer resets. Example: a search-box autocomplete that only fires the API call 300ms after the user stops typing.

Throttle ensures a function runs at most once per specified time interval, regardless of how many times the event fires. Example: limiting a scroll or resize handler to run at most once every 100ms.

questions.question: Difference between localStorage and sessionStorage
questions.answer:
Both are synchronous, string-only, origin-scoped browser storage APIs with roughly 5–10MB limits (varies by browser).

localStorage persists indefinitely — even after the browser is closed and reopened — until explicitly cleared, and is shared across all tabs of the same origin.

sessionStorage persists only for the duration of the current tab's session — closing that tab clears it, and it is not shared across tabs even for the same origin.

questions.question: Explain browser caching strategies with examples.
questions.answer:
HTTP caching is primarily controlled via response headers. Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds> tells the browser to reuse a resource without contacting the server until it expires.

ETag/Last-Modified support conditional requests (If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since) so the browser can revalidate with the server and get a cheap 304 Not Modified instead of re-downloading unchanged content.

Cache-Control: no-cache forces revalidation on every request; no-store disables caching entirely. Common strategy: serve versioned/hashed static assets with a very long max-age, and serve HTML with no-cache so users always get the latest entry point.

questions.question: How do service workers improve frontend applications?
questions.answer:
A service worker is a JavaScript file that runs in a separate thread, sitting between the web app and the network as a programmable proxy.

It can intercept fetch requests and serve cached responses, enabling offline functionality, faster repeat loads (cache-first strategies), background sync, and push notifications — the core technology behind Progressive Web Apps (PWAs). It runs independently of any open page and has no access to the DOM.

questions.question: Explain accessibility (a11y) best practices in frontend development.
questions.answer:
• Use semantic HTML elements (<button>, <nav>, <header>) instead of generic <div>s with click handlers, so assistive technology understands structure and behavior for free.
  • Ensure all interactive elements are keyboard-operable (tab order, focus states, Enter/Space activation).
  • Provide meaningful alt text for images and labels for form inputs.
  • Use ARIA attributes only when semantic HTML alone can't convey the needed meaning — "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA."
  • Maintain sufficient color contrast (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text) and don't rely on color alone to convey information.
  • Test with screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA) and automated tools (axe, Lighthouse).

questions.question: Explain React Fiber architecture.
questions.answer:
Fiber is React's internal reconciliation engine (introduced in React 16), rewritten to make rendering interruptible.

Instead of processing the entire component tree synchronously in one pass (the old "stack" reconciler, which could block the main thread on large trees), Fiber breaks rendering work into small units (one "fiber" node per component) that can be paused, resumed, aborted, or prioritized.

This enables concurrent rendering, time-slicing, and giving higher priority to user input (like typing) over lower-priority updates.

questions.question: How does React reconciliation work internally?
questions.answer:
When state or props change, React builds a new element tree ("virtual DOM") describing what the UI should look like, and diffs it against the previous tree using heuristics rather than a full tree comparison.

Key heuristics: elements of different types produce entirely different trees (old subtree torn down); elements of the same type keep their DOM node and only update changed attributes; lists use the key prop to match items across renders so React can detect insertions/removals/reorders efficiently.

React then works out an efficient set of real DOM mutations (a heuristic result, not a guaranteed-minimal diff) and applies them in a batch ("commit" phase).

questions.question: What are stale closures in React?
questions.answer:
A stale closure happens when a function (often inside useEffect, a callback, or an event handler) captures a variable's value from a particular render and continues to use that old value even after state has since updated, because the function was created during a render where that state had its old value baked in.

Commonly hit with setInterval/setTimeout inside useEffect with an empty dependency array. Fixes: use the functional form of the state setter (setCount(c => c + 1)), add correct dependencies to useEffect/useCallback, or use a ref to always read the latest value.

questions.question: Explain controlled vs. uncontrolled components.
questions.answer:
A controlled component has its form value driven entirely by React state — the input's value prop is set from state, and every change goes through an onChange handler that updates that state, making React the single source of truth.

An uncontrolled component lets the DOM itself hold the current value, and React reads it only when needed (typically via a ref).

Controlled components give more control and easier validation/formatting; uncontrolled components involve less code and can be simpler for basic forms or integrating non-React code.

questions.question: What are useMemo, useCallback, and useRef? When should you use each?
questions.answer:
useMemo(fn, deps) memoizes the result of an expensive computation, recomputing it only when a dependency changes — use it to avoid recalculating a costly derived value on every render.

useCallback(fn, deps) memoizes the function reference itself, returning the same function instance across renders unless dependencies change — useful to prevent unnecessary re-renders of memoized child components (React.memo) or to keep a stable reference for a useEffect dependency.

useRef returns a mutable object ({ current: value }) that persists across renders without causing a re-render when changed — used for accessing DOM nodes directly, or storing any mutable value that shouldn't trigger a re-render.

Note that React Compiler (stable 1.0 since October 2025) memoizes components and hooks automatically at build time, so in modern codebases manual useMemo/useCallback are mostly an escape hatch — for example, to keep a value stable when it is an effect dependency — rather than something to add everywhere. Measure before memoizing manually.

questions.question: How do you handle prop drilling when 20+ props are passed through multiple components?
questions.answer:
The core fix is to stop passing data through components that don't need it. Options, roughly in order of scope:

  • Use React's Context API so deeply nested components read shared data directly without every intermediate component forwarding it.
  • Lift shared logic into a global state manager (Redux, Zustand, Jotai) when many unrelated parts of the tree need the same data.
  • Use component composition (passing children or render props) so a parent doesn't need to know about every prop a deeply nested child needs.
  • Colocate state closer to where it's actually used instead of hoisting it too high in the first place.

questions.question: How would you design state management for large applications?
questions.answer:
Separate state by scope and lifetime rather than putting everything in one global store: local UI state (a toggle, form input) stays in component state; state shared across a few related components uses lifted state or Context.

Server/remote data (API responses) is handled by a dedicated data-fetching/caching library (React Query, SWR, RTK Query) rather than manually synced into global state, since it has its own concerns (caching, revalidation, loading/error states).

Truly global client state (auth, theme, cross-cutting UI state) goes into a lightweight global store (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai). This separation avoids unnecessary re-renders and keeps each state's lifecycle logic in the right place.

questions.question: How does React batching improve rendering?
questions.answer:
Batching groups multiple state updates that happen within the same event handler (or, since React 18, within promises, timeouts, and native event handlers too — "automatic batching") into a single re-render instead of triggering a separate re-render for each setState call.

This avoids redundant renders and layout work; e.g. calling three setStates inside one click handler still results in only one render, not three.

questions.question: What causes memory leaks in React apps?
questions.answer:
• Not cleaning up subscriptions, timers, WebSocket connections, observers, or event listeners in a useEffect cleanup function.
  • Long-lived async operations (fetch calls, polling) whose callbacks keep references to large objects after the component has unmounted — cancel them with AbortController. (Calling setState after unmount is harmless in React 18+ and the old warning was removed; the real cost is the retained work and references.)
  • Retaining references to DOM nodes or large objects in closures or module-level variables that never get released.
  • Detached DOM nodes — removing an element from the DOM tree while a JS reference to it (in state or a ref) still exists.

questions.question: How do you avoid unnecessary re-renders?
questions.answer:
Wrap components in React.memo so they skip re-rendering when their props haven't changed (shallow comparison); use useMemo/useCallback to keep object/array/function props referentially stable so React.memo comparisons actually succeed.

Split large components into smaller ones so a state change only re-renders the part of the tree that depends on it; avoid creating new objects/arrays/inline functions inside JSX props on every render; use React DevTools Profiler to identify which components are re-rendering and why before optimizing.

Also note that React Compiler can now memoize automatically at build time, so manual memoization should follow measurement rather than be applied by default.

questions.question: A dashboard has 30+ components, and changing one filter causes most of the components to re-render. How would you identify unnecessary re-renders and optimize it?
questions.answer:
First, use React DevTools Profiler (with "Highlight updates when components render" enabled) to record an interaction and see exactly which components re-rendered and why.

Common root cause: the filter state lives in a shared parent/context, and every consumer of that context re-renders whenever any value in it changes, even if a given component only cares about one field.

Fixes: split the context into smaller, more granular contexts so components only subscribe to what they need; wrap expensive child components in React.memo with stable props (using useCallback/useMemo for anything passed down); and scope filtering/derived logic to only the components that render the filtered data.

questions.question: A page needs to display 50,000 records in a table; the initial load is slow, scrolling is laggy, and filtering freezes the UI. How would you approach optimizing it (virtualization/windowing)?
questions.answer:
The DOM should never hold 50,000 real rows — only render the rows currently visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer), using a virtualization/windowing library like react-window or @tanstack/react-virtual, which recycles a small pool of DOM nodes as the user scrolls.

For the initial load, paginate or fetch data incrementally from the server instead of loading all 50,000 records at once.

For filtering, move CPU-heavy filtering logic off the main thread if needed (a Web Worker), debounce filter input so it doesn't recompute on every keystroke, and ensure the filtered result is still rendered through the virtualized list rather than a full re-render of all rows.

questions.question: How do you implement infinite scrolling efficiently?
questions.answer:
Use the IntersectionObserver API to detect when a sentinel element near the bottom of the list enters the viewport, and fetch the next page of data at that point — far more efficient than listening to scroll events and calculating positions manually.

Combine this with virtualization if the total accumulated list can grow very large, so old off-screen items don't stay in the DOM indefinitely, and guard against firing multiple fetches if the observer triggers rapidly.

questions.question: How do you optimize bundle size in React (code splitting, dynamic imports)?
questions.answer:
Use React.lazy() combined with dynamic import() to split code by route or by heavy feature, so users only download the JavaScript needed for the page they're on, loaded on demand behind a Suspense boundary.

Analyze the bundle with a tool like webpack-bundle-analyzer or vite-bundle-visualizer to find and remove/replace large dependencies, ensure tree-shaking is working (use ES modules, import only what's needed — e.g. import debounce from 'lodash/debounce' instead of the whole lodash package), and lazy-load below-the-fold or rarely-used components (modals, admin panels).

questions.question: Explain lazy loading and tree shaking.
questions.answer:
Lazy loading defers loading a resource (a component, an image, a route's JS bundle) until it's actually needed, rather than upfront — reducing initial load time.

Tree shaking is a build-time optimization (performed by bundlers like Webpack/Rollup/esbuild) that statically analyzes ES module import/export statements and removes code that is never actually used, so unused exports from a library don't end up in the final bundle.

Tree shaking requires ES modules (not CommonJS require) because static import/export can be analyzed without running the code.

questions.question: How would you optimize an eCommerce product listing page?
questions.answer:
Use server-side rendering or static generation for the initial product grid so it's fast and crawlable (SEO), lazy-load product images with proper width/height or aspect-ratio to avoid layout shift, and use responsive images (srcset) in a modern format (WebP/AVIF).

Paginate or virtualize the product list rather than rendering thousands of items at once, debounce filter/sort interactions, cache category/API responses (CDN or HTTP caching), and prioritize loading above-the-fold content first while deferring things like reviews widgets or recommendation carousels.

questions.question: How would you optimize a slow-loading React app?
questions.answer:
Measure first (Lighthouse, Web Vitals, React Profiler) to find the actual bottleneck rather than guessing.

Typical levers: code-split by route, reduce and compress the JS/CSS bundle, lazy-load non-critical components and images, use a CDN and proper HTTP caching for static assets, minimize network waterfalls (parallelize/batch API calls), memoize expensive renders and computations, server-render or pre-render content where possible, and eliminate render-blocking resources in the <head>.

questions.question: Difference between CSR and SSR?
questions.answer:
In Client-Side Rendering (CSR), the server sends a mostly empty HTML shell plus a JavaScript bundle; the browser downloads and executes the JS to render the actual content — good for highly interactive apps, but slower first paint and weaker SEO without extra tooling.

In Server-Side Rendering (SSR), the server renders the full HTML for each request before sending it to the browser, so the user sees content immediately, and then JavaScript "hydrates" the page to make it interactive.

questions.question: Difference between SSR, CSR, SSG, ISR, and hydration?
questions.answer:
CSR renders entirely in the browser after JS loads. SSR renders HTML on the server per-request, every time. SSG (Static Site Generation) renders HTML once at build time, serving the same static file to every visitor.

ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration, a feature popularized by Next.js rather than part of React itself) is a hybrid: pages are statically generated like SSG, but can be automatically regenerated in the background after a set time interval or on-demand, keeping content reasonably fresh without a full rebuild.

Hydration, common to SSR/SSG/ISR, is the process of the browser taking the server-rendered static HTML and "attaching" React's event listeners and internal state to it, turning static markup into an interactive app.

questions.question: Explain hydration mismatch and why it happens.
questions.answer:
A hydration mismatch occurs when the HTML that React renders on the client during hydration doesn't match the HTML the server actually sent — React expects them to be identical so it can reuse the existing DOM nodes.

Common causes: using browser-only APIs (window, localStorage, Date.now(), random values) during render, which produce different output on server vs. client; conditionally rendering content based on something not available at SSR time; or invalid HTML nesting that the browser silently "fixes."

React typically logs a warning and falls back to re-rendering the mismatched content on the client, hurting performance and sometimes causing a visible flicker.

questions.question: How do you cancel ongoing API requests in React (AbortController)?
questions.answer:
Create an AbortController inside useEffect, pass its signal to fetch(), and call controller.abort() in the effect's cleanup function.

This way, if the component unmounts or a dependency changes before the request finishes, the in-flight request is cancelled — preventing state updates on an unmounted component and avoiding race conditions where an older, slower request's response overwrites a newer one's.

questions.question: Explain optimistic UI updates.
questions.answer:
An optimistic update immediately updates the UI to reflect the expected result of an action (e.g. a "like" button turning blue) before the server has actually confirmed success, assuming the request will typically succeed — making the app feel instant.

If the request later fails, the UI is rolled back to its previous state and an error is shown. This trades a small risk of a visible rollback for much snappier perceived performance on the common (successful) path.

questions.question: Explain race conditions in frontend applications.
questions.answer:
A race condition happens when the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing/order of asynchronous operations — e.g. a user types "a" then quickly "ab" in a search box, firing two API requests, but the response for "a" arrives after the response for "ab" and overwrites the more relevant results.

Fixes include cancelling the previous request when a new one starts (AbortController), ignoring stale responses by tagging each request with an identifier/timestamp and discarding out-of-order results, or using a data-fetching library (React Query, SWR) that handles request deduplication and cancellation automatically.

questions.question: How would you architect a scalable frontend application?
questions.answer:
Organize code by feature/domain rather than by file type, keep a clear separation between UI components, business logic, and data-fetching layers, and use a design system/component library for consistency.

Choose state management tools appropriate to each kind of state (local, shared, server, global), enforce code quality with TypeScript/linting/tests, set up code splitting and lazy loading from the start, and establish clear conventions (routing, error boundaries, API layer) so the codebase stays maintainable as the team and feature set grow.

questions.question: Micro Frontend Architecture in Angular
questions.answer:
Micro frontends split a large frontend application into smaller, independently developed and deployed applications, each owned by a different team, then composed together into a single experience for the user — analogous to microservices on the backend.

In Angular, this is commonly implemented with Webpack Module Federation (allowing separately built Angular apps/bundles to share code and be loaded into a shell/host app at runtime) or Native Federation, letting each team ship independently while presenting one cohesive UI.

questions.question: NgRx state management: Actions & Reducers
questions.answer:
NgRx is a popular community-maintained, Redux-inspired state management library for Angular, built on RxJS (a third-party package, not part of Angular core).

An Action is a plain object describing "what happened" (a type string plus optional payload), dispatched from components or effects. A Reducer is a pure function that takes the current state and an action, and returns a new state object based on that action's type — it never mutates the existing state directly.

The store holds a single, centralized state tree, and components subscribe to slices of it (via selectors) to reactively receive updates whenever a relevant reducer produces new state.

questions.question: RxJS reactive patterns: switchMap() vs. other flattening operators
questions.answer:
These are RxJS "flattening" operators used when an Observable's value itself needs to be mapped to another Observable (e.g. an input's keystroke triggering an API call).

switchMap cancels the previous inner Observable and switches to the new one whenever the source emits again — ideal for typeahead search. mergeMap (flatMap) runs all inner Observables concurrently without cancelling earlier ones — useful when every request's result matters.

concatMap queues inner Observables and runs them strictly one after another, preserving order. exhaustMap ignores new source emissions while an inner Observable is still active — useful for preventing duplicate submit-button clicks.

questions.question: Angular Signals and fine-grained reactivity
questions.answer:
Signals are a reactive primitive that wraps a value and notifies consumers precisely when that value changes — you read one by calling it (count()) and change it with .set() or .update(). They were introduced in developer preview in Angular 16; signal() and computed() became stable in Angular 17, and effect(), linkedSignal(), and toSignal() followed in Angular 20.

Reading a signal inside a template or a computed() automatically tracks it as a dependency, so Angular updates only the specific DOM bindings that depend on that exact signal — more efficient than Angular's traditional zone.js-driven dirty-checking, which had to re-evaluate much more of the component tree on any change.

Signals are also what make zoneless change detection practical: it became stable in Angular 20.2 and is the default for new applications from Angular 21.

questions.question: What is Node.js?
questions.answer:
Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Google's V8 engine that lets JavaScript run outside the browser — on servers, CLIs, and desktop tools.

It adds capabilities V8 alone doesn't have, like file system access, networking, and an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model (via libuv), making it well suited for building fast, scalable network applications like APIs and real-time services.

questions.question: Why is Node.js single-threaded? Why "single-threaded" isn't the weakness beginners assume it is.
questions.answer: Node.js runs JavaScript application code on a main event-loop thread by default, which simplifies shared-state programming and makes non-blocking I/O efficient. However, Node.js is not literally limited to one OS thread: the operating system handles many network operations asynchronously, and libuv uses a worker pool for operations such as much of filesystem and certain DNS work. CPU-heavy JavaScript can still block the event loop, so use worker threads, separate processes, or another service for CPU-bound workloads.

questions.question: Blocking vs. non-blocking I/O (Why non-blocking I/O is the real reason Node.js is fast).
questions.answer:
Blocking I/O means the calling thread halts and waits until an I/O operation completes before moving to the next line of code — if you have one thread per request, that thread is idle while waiting, so handling many concurrent connections requires many threads.

Non-blocking I/O means the operation is initiated and the thread immediately continues with other work; a callback/Promise fires once the operation completes.

Node's single thread can therefore juggle thousands of concurrent I/O-bound connections efficiently, because it's rarely actually idle-waiting — this, not "being single-threaded," is the real source of Node's throughput advantage for I/O-heavy workloads.

questions.question: Advantages & limitations of Node.js: When to use it and when to be cautious.
questions.answer:
Advantages: excellent for I/O-heavy, real-time applications (APIs, chat apps, streaming) due to non-blocking I/O; single language (JavaScript/TypeScript) across frontend and backend; huge npm ecosystem; fast to prototype with.

Limitations: CPU-intensive work (image/video processing, heavy computation) blocks the single event loop and hurts all other requests unless offloaded to worker threads or a separate service; an uncaught exception or unhandled promise rejection crashes the entire process by default, dropping every in-flight request unless it is handled properly; callback-heavy code (largely mitigated today by async/await) can get messy if not disciplined.

Best suited to I/O-bound services; less ideal, without extra architecture, for heavy number-crunching workloads.

questions.question: Node.js vs. Java vs. .NET runtime paradigms.
questions.answer:
Node.js uses a single-threaded, event-driven, non-blocking I/O model — great concurrency for I/O-bound work with a small memory footprint per connection, but CPU-bound work needs explicit offloading.

Java (JVM) and .NET (CLR) traditionally use a multi-threaded model with a thread (or task) per request, giving true parallel execution of CPU-bound work out of the box, at the cost of higher per-thread memory overhead and the need to manage thread-safety explicitly.

Modern Java (virtual threads/Project Loom) and .NET (Task-based asynchrony) have both moved toward lighter-weight concurrency models that narrow this gap, but the underlying paradigm difference — Node's cooperative single-thread event loop vs. the JVM/CLR's preemptive multi-threading — still shapes how each ecosystem's applications are architected.

questions.question: Real-world production adoption: How companies like Netflix, PayPal, LinkedIn, and Uber run high-throughput systems on Node.js.
questions.answer:
These companies have publicly described adopting Node.js primarily for I/O-heavy, high-concurrency services where its non-blocking model shines.

PayPal reported significantly faster development and response times after moving parts of their web app to Node. Netflix uses it for its server-rendered UI layer to reduce startup time and simplify the JS toolchain between client and server.

LinkedIn used it to power their mobile backend, citing improved performance and reduced server count versus their prior stack. Uber uses Node.js in parts of its real-time dispatch system, valuing its ability to handle a very high volume of concurrent, short-lived I/O operations.

In each case, Node.js is used alongside other technologies for CPU-heavy or specialized workloads — it's rarely a company's only backend technology at that scale.

These are historical, publicly documented examples; architectures evolve, so treat them as illustrations of the trade-offs rather than a description of each company's current stack.

questions.question: How to read command-line arguments in Node.js (process.argv)?
questions.answer:
process.argv is an array of strings passed to the Node process. Index 0 is the path to the Node executable, index 1 is the path to the script being run, and index 2 onward are the actual arguments the user typed.

E.g. running node app.js --port 3000 gives process.argv = ['/path/to/node', '/path/to/app.js', '--port', '3000']. For more robust parsing (flags, defaults, help text), developers typically use a library like commander or yargs.

questions.question: Environment variables: process.env, .env, configuration, and secrets management.
questions.answer:
process.env is a Node.js object exposing the current process's environment variables, commonly used to configure behavior differently across environments without changing code.

A .env file (loaded via a package like dotenv, or natively with Node's --env-file flag or process.loadEnvFile() in recent versions) lets developers define these variables locally in a simple KEY=value format — but .env files should never be committed to version control, since they typically hold secrets like database credentials and API keys.

In production, secrets are usually injected via the hosting platform's environment variable settings or a dedicated secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) rather than a .env file.

questions.question: Path module: Resolving file and directory paths using join(), resolve(), basename(), and dirname().
questions.answer:
Node's built-in path module handles filesystem paths in an OS-independent way (Windows uses \, POSIX uses /).

path.join(...segments) joins path segments together and normalizes the result, but does not guarantee an absolute path. path.resolve(...segments) also joins segments but always returns an absolute path, resolving from right to left.

path.basename(p) returns the last portion of a path (the filename). path.dirname(p) returns the directory portion of a path.

questions.question: File System (fs): Reading, writing, updating, and deleting files asynchronously.
questions.answer:
Node's fs module (and fs/promises for a Promise-based API) provides both synchronous and asynchronous methods.

Reading: fs.promises.readFile(path, 'utf-8'). Writing (overwrite): fs.promises.writeFile(path, data). Updating/appending: fs.promises.appendFile(path, data). Deleting: fs.promises.unlink(path).

The async versions are strongly preferred in server code, since the synchronous versions block the entire event loop until the disk operation completes.

questions.question: Buffers & Streams: Handling raw binary data, files, streams, and network buffers.
questions.answer:
A Buffer is Node's way of representing raw binary data in memory, used when handling file contents, TCP packets, or image data before it's decoded into text.

A Stream is an abstraction for reading or writing data incrementally, in chunks, instead of loading an entire resource into memory at once — crucial for large files or network data.

Node has four stream types: Readable (a source), Writable (a destination), Duplex (both, e.g. a TCP socket), and Transform (a duplex stream that modifies data as it passes through, e.g. gzip compression). Streams can be chained with .pipe(), with automatic backpressure handling.

questions.question: HTTP module: Creating low-level HTTP servers and request/response streaming.
questions.answer:
Node's built-in http module lets you create an HTTP server without any framework: http.createServer((req, res) => { ... }).listen(port).

Both req (a Readable stream) and res (a Writable stream) are streams — meaning you can read a request body incrementally as it arrives and write a response incrementally, which is how frameworks like Express are built on top of this lower-level module.

questions.question: What are child processes in Node.js? Process isolation and concurrency using exec, fork, and spawn.
questions.answer:
The child_process module lets Node run other programs or additional Node scripts outside the main process, useful for CPU-intensive work or running external commands without blocking the event loop.

exec(command) runs a shell command and buffers its entire output in memory before returning it via callback. spawn(command, args) launches a command and streams its stdout/stderr incrementally — better for long-running processes or large output.

fork(modulePath) is a specialized version of spawn for launching another Node.js script as a separate process, automatically setting up an IPC channel — commonly used to offload CPU-heavy work to a separate process while keeping the main server responsive.

Note that these create separate processes, each with its own memory and V8 instance — not threads. For true multithreading inside a single process (with the option to share memory via SharedArrayBuffer), Node provides the worker_threads module.

questions.question: Need for Express.js vs. Node's raw HTTP module.
questions.answer:
Node's raw http module is very low-level — you'd have to manually parse URLs and query strings, match routes with string comparisons, parse request bodies, and write repetitive boilerplate for every endpoint.

Express provides a thin, unopinionated layer on top that handles routing, middleware composition, request/response helper methods (res.json(), req.params), and a large ecosystem of plug-in middleware — dramatically reducing boilerplate while staying close to the underlying http module's model.

questions.question: What is Express.js, and how does a request flow through Node.js + Express?
questions.answer:
Express is a minimal, flexible web framework for Node.js used to build APIs and web servers.

A request flows: the underlying http server receives the raw request → Express wraps req/res with its enhanced API → the request passes through the configured middleware stack in registration order (each middleware can inspect/modify the request, respond directly, or call next()) → Express matches the request's method and path against defined routes → the matching route handler executes and sends a response → if an error is thrown or passed to next(err), control skips ahead to the error-handling middleware, and if no route matches at all, Express's default 404 handler responds (unless you add your own catch-all middleware).

questions.question: Routing, HTTP methods, and Express Router.
questions.answer:
Express routes map an HTTP method + URL pattern to a handler function: app.get('/users', handler), app.post('/users', handler), and similarly for PUT, PATCH, DELETE. Route paths can include parameters (/users/:id, accessible via req.params.id).

express.Router() creates a mini, modular, mountable route handler — letting you group related routes into their own file/module, then attach it to the main app with app.use('/users', usersRouter), keeping large applications organized.

questions.question: Middleware architecture: How next() works and types of middleware.
questions.answer:
Middleware functions have the signature (req, res, next) and execute in the order they're registered, each getting a chance to run code, modify req/res, end the request-response cycle, or call next() to pass control to the next middleware. If next() is never called and no response is sent, the request hangs.

Types include: application-level (app.use(...)), router-level, built-in (express.json(), express.static()), third-party (cors, helmet, morgan), and error-handling middleware, distinguished by having four parameters: (err, req, res, next).

questions.question: Request & Response objects.
questions.answer:
The req (Request) object represents the incoming HTTP request and exposes properties like req.params (route parameters), req.query (query string), req.body (parsed body, needs a body-parsing middleware), req.headers, and req.method.

The res (Response) object builds and sends the response back to the client, with methods like res.send(), res.json(), res.status(code), res.set(), and res.redirect(). Both are enhanced versions of Node's raw http.IncomingMessage and http.ServerResponse objects.

questions.question: MVC (Model-View-Controller) architecture in Express.
questions.answer:
MVC separates an application into three concerns: the Model (data and business logic — typically database schemas/queries, e.g. Mongoose or Sequelize models), the View (what's presented to the user — in a pure API, often replaced by the JSON response shape), and the Controller (the logic connecting the two).

In an Express app, this typically means organizing code into models/, controllers/, and routes/ folders, with routes delegating to controller functions rather than embedding business logic directly in route handlers.

questions.question: Error handling patterns and global error-handling middleware.
questions.answer:
In Express 5 (the default version on npm), errors thrown in route handlers and middleware — including rejected Promises from async functions — are forwarded to the error-handling middleware automatically. In legacy Express 4, only synchronous throws are caught; errors inside async functions must be passed explicitly to next(err) or caught with a wrapper utility.

A global error-handling middleware is defined last, with four parameters (err, req, res, next), and centralizes how errors are logged and formatted into a consistent error response instead of duplicating try/catch logic in every route. A common pattern is a custom AppError class carrying a status code and message, thrown/passed from anywhere in the app.

questions.question: Writing test cases in Node.js (unit, integration, and mocking).
questions.answer:
Unit tests verify a single function or module in isolation, typically using a test runner/assertion library like Jest, Mocha+Chai, or Vitest.

Integration tests verify that multiple pieces work together correctly — e.g. using supertest to make real HTTP requests against an Express app (often against a test database) and asserting on the actual response.

Mocking replaces a real dependency (a database call, an external API) with a fake, controllable stand-in (via jest.mock(), or a library like sinon) so tests are fast, deterministic, and don't depend on external systems being available.

questions.question: How to handle database connections and connection pools in Node.js?
questions.answer:
Rather than opening a new database connection for every request (slow, and can exhaust the database's max-connections limit under load), applications use a connection pool — a set of pre-established, reusable connections managed by the database driver/ORM.

A request borrows a connection from the pool, uses it, and returns it when done; if all connections are in use, further requests queue until one is freed (or time out, which signals the pool size or query performance needs attention). Pool size should be tuned to the database's actual capacity, not set arbitrarily high.

questions.question: An API needs to make 5 independent database/API calls. Would you use Promise.all() to execute them concurrently? What problems could this cause under heavy traffic?
questions.answer:
Yes — if the 5 calls are truly independent, Promise.all() lets them run concurrently instead of sequentially, significantly reducing total response time.

Under heavy traffic, though, this multiplies the load: if 1,000 concurrent requests each fire 5 calls, that's 5,000 simultaneous downstream calls, which can exhaust a database connection pool or hit a third-party API's rate limit. Also, Promise.all() rejects as soon as any one call fails, even if the other 4 succeeded.

Mitigations: use Promise.allSettled() when partial success is acceptable, add concurrency limits/queuing (e.g. p-limit), and ensure downstream systems can actually handle the peak concurrent load this pattern generates.

questions.question: Your API works well with a small number of users but becomes extremely slow when concurrent traffic increases significantly, driving CPU usage to 100%. How would you identify the bottleneck and optimize the application?
questions.answer:
High CPU (not just high latency) under load points to CPU-bound work blocking the single event loop — common causes: synchronous, expensive computation running inline on every request, or unintentionally blocking calls (e.g. fs.readFileSync in a hot path).

To diagnose: use Node's built-in profiler (node --prof) or a tool like Clinic.js/0x to capture a CPU flame graph under load; check event loop lag with a metric like perf_hooks or a library like toobusy-js.

Fixes: move CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a separate microservice/queue; replace blocking sync calls with async equivalents; cache expensive repeated computations; and horizontally scale (more instances behind a load balancer, or Node's cluster module) since a single Node process can only use one core for JS execution.

questions.question: Java 8 features & Lambda Expressions
questions.answer:
Java 8 (2014) introduced major functional-programming features: lambda expressions ((a, b) -> a + b), a concise syntax for implementing a functional interface's single method without a full anonymous class; method references (String::length); and the Stream API for declarative, chainable collection processing.

Also: the Optional<T> class to explicitly represent a possibly-absent value and reduce NullPointerExceptions; default and static methods on interfaces; and the new java.time date/time API replacing the flawed old Date/Calendar classes.

questions.question: Functional Interfaces
questions.answer:
A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method (it may have any number of default/static methods), making it a valid target for a lambda expression or method reference.

Java's java.util.function package provides common ones: Function<T,R> (takes T, returns R), Predicate<T> (takes T, returns boolean), Consumer<T> (takes T, returns nothing), and Supplier<T> (takes nothing, returns T). The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but documents intent and causes a compile error if a second abstract method is accidentally added.

questions.question: Stream API: filter(), map(), and reduce()
questions.answer:
The Stream API processes sequences of elements declaratively through a pipeline of operations rather than explicit loops.

filter(Predicate) keeps only elements matching a condition (an intermediate, lazy operation). map(Function) transforms each element into another value/type (also intermediate/lazy). reduce(identity, BinaryOperator) is a terminal operation that combines all elements into a single result (e.g. stream.reduce(0, Integer::sum)).

Intermediate operations don't execute until a terminal operation (reduce, collect, forEach) is called, at which point the whole pipeline processes the data in a single pass.

questions.question: How HashMap works internally (buckets, hash collisions, treeification)
questions.answer:
A HashMap stores entries in an internal array of "buckets." When a key is inserted, its hashCode() is computed and run through a hash-spreading function to determine which bucket it belongs to.

When two different keys hash to the same bucket (a collision), Java (since Java 8) stores them as a linked list within that bucket by default, falling back to equals() comparisons to distinguish keys in the same bucket. If a bucket's linked list grows past a threshold (8 entries, with the table having at least 64 buckets), Java converts it to a balanced red-black tree ("treeification") to keep worst-case lookup at O(log n) instead of O(n).

The map resizes (doubling its bucket array and rehashing everything) once entries exceed capacity × loadFactor (default load factor 0.75).

questions.question: HashMap vs. ConcurrentHashMap
questions.answer:
HashMap is not thread-safe — concurrent modification from multiple threads can corrupt its internal structure or produce inconsistent reads, without throwing an error to warn you.

ConcurrentHashMap is designed for safe concurrent access without needing to synchronize the entire map: instead of locking the whole structure on every write (like the older Hashtable or a manually-synchronized HashMap), it uses fine-grained locking (historically per-segment, now largely per-bucket/CAS-based in modern JDKs) so multiple threads can read and write different parts of the map concurrently, giving much better throughput under contention while still guaranteeing thread safety.

questions.question: Spring Boot & Dependency Injection
questions.answer:
Spring Boot is an opinionated framework built on top of the Spring Framework that dramatically simplifies setting up a production-ready Spring application — auto-configuration, an embedded server (Tomcat by default), starter dependencies, and minimal XML/boilerplate configuration.

Dependency Injection (DI) is Spring's core design pattern: rather than a class creating its own dependencies, it declares what it needs (via constructor, field, or setter injection), and the Spring container is responsible for constructing and "injecting" those dependencies at runtime. This decouples classes from the concrete construction of their collaborators, making code easier to test and maintain.

questions.question: Inversion of Control (IoC) container & @Autowired
questions.answer:
Inversion of Control is the broader principle behind DI: control over object creation and wiring is inverted from the application code to a framework/container. Spring's IoC container (the ApplicationContext) is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and managing the lifecycle of "beans" based on configuration.

@Autowired tells Spring to automatically inject a matching bean into a field, constructor, or setter — Spring resolves it by type (and by name/qualifier if there are multiple candidates) from beans already registered in the container. Constructor injection is generally preferred over field injection, since it makes dependencies explicit and required, and works better with immutability and testing.

questions.question: Spring Bean vs. JavaBean lifecycle
questions.answer:
A JavaBean is a plain Java class convention: a no-argument constructor, private fields with public getters/setters — just a naming/structure convention, unrelated to any framework.

A Spring Bean is any object that is instantiated, configured, and managed by the Spring IoC container (regardless of whether it follows JavaBean conventions). Its lifecycle: the container instantiates it → dependencies are injected → any @PostConstruct-annotated method runs → the bean is ready for use → on container shutdown, any @PreDestroy-annotated method runs for cleanup.

By default, Spring beans are singletons (one shared instance per container), though other scopes (prototype, request, session) are available.

questions.question: REST APIs & HTTP methods in Spring: PUT vs. PATCH
questions.answer:
In REST conventions (Spring's @PutMapping/@PatchMapping), PUT is used to replace an entire resource — the client sends the full representation, and PUT is defined to be idempotent (calling it multiple times with the same payload produces the same result).

PATCH is used for a partial update — the client sends only the fields that should change, and other existing fields are left untouched. PATCH is not guaranteed to be idempotent depending on how it's implemented.

questions.question: Data persistence: CrudRepository vs. JpaRepository
questions.answer:
Both are Spring Data interfaces you extend to get repository methods without writing implementation code. CrudRepository<T, ID> provides the basics: save(), findById(), findAll(), deleteById(), count(), etc.

JpaRepository<T, ID> builds on top of that: in Spring Data 3.x it extends ListCrudRepository and ListPagingAndSortingRepository (note that since 3.0, PagingAndSortingRepository no longer extends CrudRepository, as it did in 2.x). It adds JPA-specific and more convenient methods: List return types instead of Iterable, batch operations (e.g. deleteAllInBatch()), flush() to force pending changes immediately, pagination (findAll(Pageable)), and sorting support.

In practice, most Spring Boot + JPA projects use JpaRepository directly for its richer feature set, reaching for the narrower CrudRepository mainly to deliberately limit the exposed API surface.

questions.question: Microservices inter-service communication patterns
questions.answer:
Services communicate either synchronously or asynchronously. Synchronous: direct HTTP/REST calls (simple, but couples the caller to the callee's availability) or gRPC (faster, strongly-typed, binary protocol, good for internal service-to-service calls).

Asynchronous: message brokers/event streaming (Kafka, RabbitMQ) where a service publishes an event and other services consume it independently, decoupling producer and consumer in time.

Choosing between them is a trade-off: synchronous calls are simpler to reason about but create tighter coupling and can cascade failures; asynchronous messaging improves resilience and scalability but adds complexity (eventual consistency, message ordering, debugging distributed flows).

questions.question: API Gateway & Service Discovery (Eureka)
questions.answer:
An API Gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of a microservices architecture, routing incoming requests to the appropriate backend service, and commonly handling cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and request logging.

Service Discovery solves the problem of services needing to find each other's current network location in a dynamic environment where instances scale up/down and IPs change. Eureka (part of Spring Cloud Netflix) is a service registry where each service instance registers itself on startup (with periodic heartbeats), and other services/the gateway query Eureka to discover healthy instances of a service by name instead of hardcoding IPs.

In Kubernetes-based deployments, the platform's built-in DNS-based service discovery often replaces a separate registry like Eureka.

questions.question: Declarative REST clients (Feign Client) & Circuit Breakers (Resilience4j / Hystrix)
questions.answer:
Feign is a declarative HTTP client — instead of manually writing HTTP call boilerplate, you define a Java interface annotated with the target endpoint's details, and Spring Cloud OpenFeign generates the implementation at runtime, making inter-service calls look like simple method calls.

A circuit breaker protects a service from repeatedly calling a dependency that's failing or slow: after a configured failure threshold, the circuit "opens" and further calls fail fast (optionally falling back to a default response) instead of piling up and waiting on a doomed call; after a cooldown period it moves to "half-open" to test if the dependency has recovered.

Hystrix was Netflix's original circuit breaker library for this pattern but was put into maintenance mode; Resilience4j is its modern, lightweight successor and the current standard choice in the Spring ecosystem.

questions.question: How do you decide between SQL (relational) and NoSQL (document/key-value)?
questions.answer:
Choose SQL (relational, e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL) when data is highly structured with clear relationships, strong consistency and transactional guarantees (ACID) matter (financial records, inventory), and you need flexible, complex querying (joins, aggregations) across normalized data.

Choose NoSQL when the data model is more flexible/nested, you need to scale horizontally across many servers more easily than relational databases traditionally allow, extreme write throughput or massive scale is a priority, or the schema is expected to evolve frequently without costly migrations.

Many real systems use both ("polyglot persistence") — a relational database for core transactional data and a NoSQL store for something like session data, logs, or a product catalog.

questions.question: What is indexing, and how do B-Trees/LSM-Trees work under the hood?
questions.answer:
An index is an auxiliary data structure that lets a database find rows matching a query without scanning the entire table, at the cost of extra storage and slightly slower writes.

A B-Tree (used by most relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL/InnoDB) is a balanced, sorted tree structure where each node can have many children, keeping the tree shallow so a lookup, insert, or range scan takes only a few disk reads (O(log n)) even for huge tables — well-suited to a mix of reads and writes.

An LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge-Tree, used by databases optimized for high write throughput, like Cassandra and RocksDB) instead buffers writes in memory and periodically flushes them to disk as immutable, sorted files, later merged/compacted in the background — trading some read complexity for much faster sequential writes.

questions.question: What is sharding, and how does horizontal partitioning differ from vertical partitioning?
questions.answer:
Sharding is splitting a large database across multiple servers so no single machine needs to hold or process all the data, enabling horizontal scalability beyond what a single server can handle.

Horizontal partitioning (what sharding typically refers to) splits a table by rows — e.g. users 1–1,000,000 on shard A, 1,000,001–2,000,000 on shard B, based on a shard key. Vertical partitioning splits a table by columns instead — e.g. frequent columns in one table, rarely-accessed large columns in another.

Sharding adds significant complexity around choosing a good shard key, cross-shard queries/joins, and rebalancing as data grows, and is usually adopted only once a single database instance genuinely can't handle the load.

questions.question: PostgreSQL: How do you approach schema design, connection pooling, and query optimization for an application with heavy read traffic?
questions.answer:
Schema design: normalize to avoid data anomalies, but selectively denormalize (or use materialized views) for read-heavy paths where joins are too expensive at scale; choose appropriate data types and constraints/foreign keys so the query planner can make better decisions.

Connection pooling: Postgres connections are relatively expensive, so use a pooler (PgBouncer, or the driver/ORM's built-in pool) sized to the database's actual capacity, rather than opening a raw connection per request.

Query optimization: use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see the actual query plan and find sequential scans that should be index scans; add indexes on frequently filtered/joined/sorted columns; consider read replicas to offload read traffic from the primary; cache frequently-read, rarely-changing data at the application layer (Redis); and keep VACUUM/ANALYZE maintenance current so the planner's statistics stay accurate.

questions.question: Express + MongoDB API integration flow.
questions.answer:
A typical flow: the Express app connects to MongoDB at startup using a driver like Mongoose (an ODM providing schemas, validation, and a query API) or the native MongoDB Node.js driver.

Incoming requests hit an Express route → a controller function → calls a Mongoose model method (User.find(), User.create(), etc.) → Mongoose translates that into a MongoDB query over the existing connection → the result is returned up through the controller and sent back as a JSON response via res.json().

Connection setup typically happens once at app startup, and Mongoose/the driver manages an internal connection pool automatically.

questions.question: Your collection has 50+ million documents and a frequently used query is taking several seconds. How would you identify the bottleneck (explain()) and design the right compound index (ESR rule)?
questions.answer:
Run the query with explain("executionStats") and inspect stages such as COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN, nReturned, totalDocsExamined, totalKeysExamined, and execution time. A large examined-to-returned ratio is a signal that the plan may be inefficient.

For compound indexes, Equality-Sort-Range (ESR) is a useful guideline when preserving index-supported sort order matters: equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields. It is not an absolute law; if a range predicate is highly selective, an ERS order can be better. Test realistic candidates with explain() and verify the plan after deployment.

questions.question: An aggregation pipeline using $match, $lookup, $unwind, $sort, and $group is taking 8â€“10 seconds. How would you analyze and optimize it?
questions.answer:
Use .explain() on the aggregation to see each stage's execution stats and find which stage is consuming the most time/documents.

  • Put $match (and $sort, where possible) as early in the pipeline as possible so later stages process far fewer documents, and ensure fields used in an early $match are indexed.
  • $lookup (a join) is often the most expensive stage — ensure the foreign field is indexed on the target collection, and consider embedding data instead of referencing it if this join happens on every query.
  • $unwind can multiply document count dramatically — only unwind when necessary, and do it after filtering down with $match.
  • $group generally cannot use an index itself (the main exception is a $sort on the group key followed by a $group that uses only $first, which can use a DISTINCT_SCAN), so shrink its input with an indexed $match first, and consider a pre-aggregated/materialized collection updated on write to avoid recomputing this pipeline on every read.

questions.question: Explain authentication vs. authorization.
questions.answer:
Authentication answers "who are you?" — verifying a user's identity, typically via credentials like a username/password, a token, or biometrics.

Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" — determining, once identity is established, what resources or actions that authenticated user is permitted to access. They're sequential: authentication must happen first, and authorization decisions are then made based on the authenticated identity.

questions.question: How can we implement authentication and authorization in Node.js?
questions.answer:
A common approach: store hashed passwords (using bcrypt or argon2, never plaintext) at registration; on login, verify the submitted password against the stored hash, then issue a token — commonly a JWT signed by the server, or a session ID stored server-side with a cookie referencing it.

Middleware (e.g. using passport.js, or custom middleware) then verifies that token/session on subsequent requests, attaching the authenticated user to req.user. Authorization is layered on top — middleware checking req.user's role or permissions before allowing access to a given route, or more granular per-resource checks inside the route handler itself.

questions.question: Explain CORS in simple terms and how browser preflight (OPTIONS) works.
questions.answer:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that, by default, blocks a web page from making requests to a different origin than the one it was served from, unless the target server explicitly allows it via response headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin, etc.).

For "simple" (CORS-safelisted) requests, the browser just sends the request and checks the response headers to decide whether to expose the response to the calling JavaScript. For requests that aren't CORS-safelisted (methods like PUT/DELETE, custom or Authorization headers, or a Content-Type of application/json), the browser first sends an automatic "preflight" OPTIONS request to ask the server if the actual request would be allowed — only if confirmed does the browser send the real request.

questions.question: How do refresh tokens work internally?
questions.answer:
An access token is typically short-lived (minutes) to limit the damage if it's stolen, but that means the user would otherwise have to re-login frequently.

A refresh token is a separate, longer-lived credential issued alongside the access token at login, stored more securely (often an HttpOnly cookie), and used only to request a new access token from a dedicated endpoint once the current one expires — it is not sent with every regular API request.

The server verifies the refresh token (checking it against a stored/allow-listed value, since refresh tokens are typically revocable, unlike a pure stateless JWT) and, if valid, issues a new access token.

questions.question: Explain JWT authentication end-to-end with the refresh token rotation flow.
questions.answer:
On login, the server verifies credentials and issues a short-lived JWT access token (signed, containing claims like user ID and expiry) plus a long-lived refresh token, and both are sent to the client.

The client sends the access token (e.g. in an Authorization: Bearer <token> header) with each API request; the server verifies its signature and expiry without needing a database lookup (in a purely stateless design — many systems still check revocation lists or user status). When the access token expires, the client calls a /refresh endpoint with the refresh token.

With rotation, each time the refresh token is used, the server invalidates it and issues both a brand-new access token and a brand-new refresh token — if an old, already-used refresh token is ever presented again, the server treats it as a signal of possible theft and can revoke the entire token family, forcing re-login.

questions.question: How do you securely store tokens in frontend applications (HttpOnly cookies vs. in-memory)?
questions.answer:
Storing tokens in localStorage/sessionStorage is convenient but exposes them to any XSS vulnerability — malicious injected JavaScript can simply read localStorage and exfiltrate the token.

An HttpOnly cookie (with Secure and SameSite attributes) cannot be read by JavaScript at all, so an XSS attack cannot exfiltrate the token itself (though injected scripts can still make authenticated requests while the page is open), and it brings its own consideration (CSRF, mitigated with SameSite=Strict/Lax and/or CSRF tokens).

Storing the access token in memory only (a JS variable, not persisted) is another common pattern — it disappears on page refresh (requiring a silent refresh via an HttpOnly refresh-token cookie), which limits its exposure window. A common secure pattern: refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; access token kept only in memory on the client.

questions.question: Explain frontend security vulnerabilities developers must protect against (XSS, CSRF, Clickjacking).
questions.answer:
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is when an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page, which then runs in victims' browsers with full access to that page's cookies/DOM — prevented by escaping/sanitizing all user-generated content before rendering, using a framework that escapes by default (React does, unless using dangerouslySetInnerHTML), and setting a Content-Security-Policy header.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into unknowingly submitting a request to another site where they're authenticated (since browsers automatically attach cookies) — prevented with CSRF tokens and/or the SameSite cookie attribute.

Clickjacking tricks a user into clicking something different from what they perceive (e.g. an invisible iframe overlaid on an attacker's page) — prevented with the X-Frame-Options header or a Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors directive.

questions.question: How do you secure your APIs against bots, abuse, and common attacks (rate limiting, input sanitization, security headers)?
questions.answer:
Rate limiting (e.g. express-rate-limit, or at the infrastructure/API-gateway level) caps how many requests a given IP/user/API key can make in a time window, protecting against brute-force login attempts and abusive scraping/bots.

Input validation (schema validation with something like zod or joi) rejects malformed data early, but injection is prevented by keeping data separate from code: parameterized queries for SQL/NoSQL, and output encoding for HTML. Security headers (via a library like helmet) add protections like disabling X-Powered-By, enforcing HTTPS (Strict-Transport-Security), and setting a Content-Security-Policy.

Additional layers: requiring API keys/authentication for sensitive endpoints, CAPTCHAs on public forms prone to bot abuse, and a WAF or CDN-level bot protection in front of the API.

questions.question: Protected routes implementation across frontend and backend.
questions.answer:
On the backend, this is enforced with authentication middleware placed in front of protected route handlers — the middleware checks for a valid token/session, and rejects the request (401 Unauthorized) before it reaches the actual route logic if the check fails; this is the layer that actually matters for security.

On the frontend, a "protected route" wrapper component checks whether the user is authenticated before rendering the intended page, redirecting to a login page otherwise — but this is purely a UX convenience, not a real security boundary, since any frontend check can be bypassed by someone calling the API directly; the backend check is what actually protects the data.

questions.question: Why Node.js is suitable for scalable applications.
questions.answer:
Node's non-blocking, event-driven I/O model lets a single process handle a very large number of concurrent connections efficiently for I/O-bound workloads (typical of web APIs, which spend most of their time waiting on database/network calls, not computing) — without the memory overhead of a thread per connection.

It scales horizontally easily (running multiple stateless Node instances behind a load balancer, or using the cluster module/pm2 to use multiple CPU cores on one machine), and its huge npm ecosystem and JSON-native data handling make it a natural fit for building and rapidly iterating on scalable REST/GraphQL APIs.

questions.question: How do you design REST APIs that stay secure and stable under high concurrent traffic (auth, rate limiting, caching)?
questions.answer:
Auth: use stateless authentication (JWTs) where possible so any server instance can validate a request without a shared session store bottleneck, or use a fast, centralized session store (Redis) if stateful sessions are required.

Rate limiting: apply per-user/per-IP limits (locally or via a shared store like Redis so limits are consistent across multiple server instances) to prevent any single client from degrading service for others.

Caching: cache expensive or frequently-requested, rarely-changing responses (CDN caching, Redis, proper HTTP cache headers) so repeated requests don't all hit the database/application logic. Beyond that: horizontal scaling behind a load balancer, connection pooling, circuit breakers around slow downstream dependencies, and load/stress testing before launch.

questions.question: Your app handles 1M+ daily views during a flash sale spike â€” walk through how you would optimize load time, add CDN caching, and prevent downtime.
questions.answer:
First, translate "views" into peak load: 1M views per day averages only about 12 requests/second, but a flash sale can compress much of that into minutes (1M views in 10 minutes is roughly 1,700 requests/second, and each view usually triggers several requests), so design against peak requests/second, concurrent users, and a latency target rather than the daily total.

Serve static assets (JS, CSS, images, and even static/rarely-changing HTML) through a CDN, so most requests never reach the origin server. Cache API responses that don't need to be real-time (e.g. product catalog data) at the CDN or application layer (Redis), with a short TTL.

Pre-warm caches and autoscale server capacity ahead of the expected spike rather than reactively, since autoscaling has ramp-up latency. Add rate limiting/a queueing system (e.g. a virtual waiting room) for the highest-contention actions (like checkout for a limited-stock item) to prevent the backend/database from being overwhelmed.
